NgraceChangeDesignContext.Rationale: `stat` device/inode can be recycled after `unlink`, so a comparison of a recorded pair against a re-read path cannot tell an object from a same-path replacement on a filesystem that recycles inode numbers. The repair therefore pins identity to the opened object: open once, record the pair with `fstat` of that handle, read the lock's ownership bytes from the same handle, and hold the handle until the destructive call. An open handle keeps the observed inode allocated, so a replacement cannot receive that number and the comparison becomes sound. `fstat` binding closes the separate-path gap that let an implementation open one object and record another after a rename, or read `readFileSync(path)` and `statSync(path)` from two different lock files. When the handle cannot be obtained the operation preserves and refuses with a named diagnostic and never substitutes the unpinned comparison, because that comparison is exactly the deletion the Linux CI observed. The ordinary `spec new` mint and handled cleanup must still succeed on a supported platform, Windows included; the Windows job is the only place a Windows platform claim is taken from. All measurements in this document are dated 2026-09-23 and were taken on Linux with Bun 1.3.14. The implementation authority independently confirmed in a separate disposable ext4 mount that unpinned file and directory replacements reused an inode 100/100 times each, versus 0/100 with the old object open.

Alternatives.Alternative: **A `birthtime` secondary instead of a handle.** Record creation time beside device/inode. Rejected: on filesystems with coarse or absent creation timestamps it cannot prove identity, so the guard would be sound only where it is not needed.
**Fall back to the unpinned `dev`/`ino` comparison when the handle cannot be opened.** Rejected: it reproduces the verified pre-pin deletion on ext4 and would delete another actor's object.

**A refusal-only Windows test.** Rejected by the authority: Windows is a supported CI platform, so the platform-agnostic success and forced-failure tests must run there, and a run whose only green is a refusal is not a pass.

**Release the pin before the final removal on every platform.** Rejected as the default: it reopens the identity window on platforms that can remove an owned object while its handle is open. It is permitted only as a last resort on a platform that cannot, closing the handle after every ownership check and immediately before the destructive call, inside the archived post-validation/pre-unlink boundary.
